hints: Relate the resistance unit to potential difference and current.
State the potential difference per ampere, or describe the resistance that gives one ampere for one volt.
walkthrough: Resistance is measured as potential difference divided by current.
One ohm is one volt per ampere.
Equivalently, an ohm is the resistance for which a potential difference of one volt produces a current of one ampere.

ai_rubric.observable: Defines an ohm as one volt per ampere, or the resistance for which one volt produces one ampere.

hints: Rearrange the resistance–resistivity equation to make the wire length the subject.
Convert the cross-sectional area from mm² to m² before substituting it into the equation.
walkthrough: Use R = ρL / A and rearrange to L = RA / ρ.
Convert the area: 0.38 mm² = 0.38 × 10⁻⁶ m².
This gives L = 0.7125 m, so the wire length is 0.71 m.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses the resistance–resistivity relationship R = ρL / A.
Rearranges to L = RA / ρ and uses 0.38 × 10⁻⁶ m² for the cross-sectional area.
Calculates the wire length as 0.71 m.

hints: Track where the energy supplied per unit charge by the battery is transferred before charge reaches resistor X.
Resistor Y is in the circuit as well, so some energy is dissipated there as thermal energy.
walkthrough: The e.m.f. is the energy transferred by the battery per unit charge around the complete circuit.
Charge passes through resistor Y as well as resistor X.
Some energy is dissipated as thermal energy in resistor Y.
Less energy per unit charge remains to be transferred in resistor X, so its p.d. is less than the battery e.m.f.

ai_rubric.observable: Explains that thermal energy is dissipated in resistor Y, leaving less energy per unit charge for resistor X.

hints: The two resistors are in series, so their resistances add and the same current passes through both.
Either use the resistance ratio for X, or find the circuit current first and then use V = IR for X.
walkthrough: The resistors are in series, so their combined resistance is 1.8 Ω + 0.60 Ω = 2.4 Ω.
The current is I = 1.2 / 2.4 = 0.50 A.
The potential difference across X is Vₓ = IRₓ = 0.50 × 1.8 = 0.90 V.
Equivalently, Vₓ / 1.2 = 1.8 / (1.8 + 0.60), giving Vₓ = 0.90 V.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses either the resistance ratio Vₓ / 1.2 = 1.8 / (1.8 + 0.60), or finds the series current as 1.2 / (1.8 + 0.60).
Calculates the potential difference across X as 0.90 V by either accepted route.

hints: Compare the potential difference across the resistor branch before and after the identical ideal battery is connected in parallel.
Both batteries maintain the same 1.2 V potential difference between the two rails.
walkthrough: Before battery Q is added, battery P provides 1.2 V across the series branch containing X and Y.
Battery Q is also an ideal 1.2 V source connected across the same two rails.
The potential difference across the resistor branch is therefore still 1.2 V.
Because the branch resistance is unchanged, the current through resistor X remains the same.

ai_rubric.observable: States that the current in resistor X remains the same.

hints: The current in the resistor branch is unchanged, but now consider how that branch current is supplied.
With two identical ideal batteries in parallel, battery Q supplies some of the current that battery P previously supplied alone.
walkthrough: The resistor branch still has the same 1.2 V potential difference, so its current is unchanged.
Before Q is connected, battery P supplies all of that branch current.
After Q is connected in parallel with P, the identical battery Q supplies part of the branch current.
The current supplied by battery P therefore decreases.

ai_rubric.observable: States that the current in battery P decreases.

hints: Use the reciprocal-resistance relationship for the 1.8 Ω and 3.6 Ω resistors in parallel.
Add 1 / 1.8 and 1 / 3.6, then invert the result to obtain the total resistance.
walkthrough: For resistors in parallel, 1 / R = 1 / R₁ + 1 / R₂.
Substitute the two parallel resistors: 1 / R = 1 / 1.8 + 1 / 3.6.
This gives 1 / R = 0.833... Ω⁻¹, so R = 1.2 Ω.
The total resistance of the two parallel resistors is 1.2 Ω.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses reciprocal resistance addition for 1.8 Ω and 3.6 Ω to obtain a combined resistance of 1.2 Ω.

hints: Use the 1.2 Ω equivalent resistance from part (e)(i), then include the 0.60 Ω resistor Y in series.
Alternatively, find the potential difference across Y from the 1.2 Ω : 0.60 Ω resistance ratio, then use I = V / R.
walkthrough: From part (e)(i), the parallel pair has equivalent resistance 1.2 Ω.
This is in series with Y, so the total resistance is 1.2 Ω + 0.60 Ω = 1.8 Ω.
The current through the series resistor Y is I = 1.2 / 1.8 = 0.667 A.
Therefore the current in Y is 0.67 A.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses either I = 1.2 / (1.2 + 0.60), or calculates Vᵧ = 1.2 × 0.60 / (1.2 + 0.60).
Calculates the current in Y as 0.67 A by either accepted route.
